rationale: B wins because it knows where the bodies are buried: “whether the 10% applies to subscriptions bought inside the iOS and Android apps” is the question that decides whether the strongest story survives. A has good instincts, but “Discord just gave server owners a way to get paid — it won't say how much they'll make” tries to make missing data carry a story by itself. That is not fatal, but it is thinner and lazier than B’s conditional customer-story frame.
gaps_in_A: “Confirmation of exactly which transactions the 10% applies to” is too soft. The real proof question is whether Apple/Google fees stack on mobile and whether payment processing is inside the 10%.

“Discord just gave server owners a way to get paid — it won't say how much they'll make” makes absence of earnings data the hook. Without a named server owner, projections, or payout mechanics, that is context, not a story.
“how this revenue stream fits alongside existing lines (ads, Nitro)” imports revenue-line specifics not supplied in the update. Do not sneak outside knowledge into a blind angle set.
“Does ‘premium content’ on gaming servers include anything gambling- or loot-box-adjacent?” is an unsupported regulatory detour. Interesting, maybe, but the facts did not earn it.
gaps_in_B: “the fee comparison is Discord's own framing” overstates the supplied facts. The update says the fee is below the app-store standard; it does not say Discord framed it that way publicly.
“The launch lands while the IPO reporting is live” turns “reportedly preparing for an IPO” into a fresher market peg than the facts prove. It needs a source/date before a markets reporter buys it.
“quiet period” is a useful caution, but a touch over-lawyered without evidence of a filing or formal IPO step. Keep it as a check, not a premise.
